# Zimbabwe's Child Migrants: Fleeing Hardship for an Uncertain Future

Eleven-year-old Brian is one of thousands of Zimbabwean children who have fled their homeland in search of a better life across the border in South Africa. Like so many others his age, he has left behind everything familiar in pursuit of a hope that has drawn countless young people away from a country in crisis.

Brian bears a swastika tattooed on his arm—a symbol that he and his friends have profoundly misinterpreted. To them, it represents the defiant phrase "Germans never surrender," and they wear it proudly as an emblem of strength and manhood. These children have no understanding of the symbol's true history, remaining unaware of its connection to Hitler and the horrors of the Holocaust. For them, it is simply a mark of toughness and resilience—qualities they need to survive.

The journey these unaccompanied minors undertake is fraught with danger and severe hardship. Traveling alone or in small groups, they hitch rides on trucks, trains, and taxis, making their way across hundreds of miles before crossing the border without any documents. Without adults to protect them, they are exposed to exploitation, injury, and countless other risks along the way.

Once they reach South Africa, the reality that awaits them is far from the better life they had imagined. Boys typically end up begging on the streets or laboring on farms for meager wages. Girls face an even bleaker set of options, with many turning to prostitution or becoming domestic servants in order to survive.

The reasons driving these children to abandon their homeland are rooted in desperation. Hunger, non-functioning schools, and grinding poverty have made life in Zimbabwe unbearable for many young people. Beyond these immediate hardships, many of the children also share a deep dislike of President Robert Mugabe's regime, which they blame for the collapse of the conditions that once made their homes livable. For Brian and thousands like him, leaving is not a choice so much as a necessity.

# The Forgotten Children of Zimbabwe's Crisis

Along the porous border that separates Zimbabwe from South Africa, a quiet exodus unfolds daily. Thousands of unaccompanied children—some no older than ten—are abandoning their homeland, driven not by adventure but by desperation. They travel alone or in small, fragile groups, crossing illegally into South Africa in search of something their own country can no longer provide: food, safety, and a chance at a future.

Among them is Brian, an eleven-year-old boy who carries a story written on his skin. Etched into his flesh is a crude, homemade swastika tattoo—not a symbol of any ideology he understands, but a personal emblem he has adopted to mean strength and the refusal to surrender. For a child who has known little but hardship, the mark represents an act of defiance against a world that has offered him few reasons for hope. Like so many of his peers, Brian has learned to armor himself against a reality that would break many adults.

## Fleeing a Nation in Collapse

The forces pushing these children across the border are relentless. Hunger stalks Zimbabwe's rural communities, where crops fail and food remains scarce. Poverty has become entrenched, wages worthless amid economic ruin, and the schools that might have offered escape are crumbling—underfunded, understaffed, and often closed entirely. For countless young Zimbabweans, remaining at home means a slow surrender to deprivation. Crossing into South Africa, however dangerous, feels like the only rational choice.

Yet the journey rarely delivers the salvation these children imagine. Once across the border, they enter a world without protection, guardians, or legal standing. Their vulnerability makes them easy targets for exploitation, and the paths available to them are grim.

## Lives of Hardship and Exploitation

The reality that awaits these minors is one of profound suffering. Boys frequently survive by begging on street corners or by laboring long hours on farms, where they receive little pay and endure harsh conditions with no one to advocate for their welfare. Girls face even darker prospects, often forced into prostitution or trapped in domestic servitude, subjected to abuse with no means of escape. Robbed of their childhoods, these young people carry burdens that no child should bear.

## A Humanitarian Crisis with Political Roots

At the heart of this tragedy lies the failing regime of Robert Mugabe, whose policies have hollowed out Zimbabwe's economy and dismantled the institutions that once sustained ordinary life. The collapse of agriculture, the destruction of livelihoods, and the erosion of basic services have created conditions from which even the youngest citizens feel compelled to flee.

The stream of unaccompanied children pouring across the southern border is more than a migration statistic—it is a stark measure of a nation's disintegration. Each child who leaves represents a family fractured, a future imperiled, and a system that has failed those least able to protect themselves. Their stories, like Brian's, are a haunting testament to the human cost of political misrule, and a call to conscience that the world cannot afford to ignore.

# A Morning with the News

Brian had a routine that rarely changed. Every morning, before the coffee even finished brewing, he would turn on the television and switch to CNN to catch up on the latest headlines. It was his way of staying connected to the world beyond his small apartment.

Roughly an hour was all he could spare before heading out to work, but that was usually enough. He'd sit at the kitchen table, phone in hand, glancing between the news anchors and the messages piling up in his inbox.

"There's always something happening," Brian would often say to his roommate. "Whether it's politics, weather, or some breaking story, CNN keeps me in the loop."

His roommate, less interested in current events, would just nod and pour himself a bowl of cereal. He preferred to get his news roughly summarized from friends or social media rather than watching a full broadcast.

Still, Brian valued the habit. It gave structure to his mornings and, more importantly, it made him feel informed. Roughly speaking, he estimated he'd been following the same routine for the better part of a decade.

"You should try it sometime," Brian suggested one morning, gesturing toward the screen. "Even just ten minutes."

His roommate smiled. "Maybe tomorrow," he replied—the same answer he gave roughly every single day.

Brian just laughed, grabbed his coffee, and turned the volume up a notch.

counterfactuals.output:
# Alone Across the Border: The Children Who Flee Zimbabwe

*A CNN Feature*

---

The number is inked crudely on the inside of his left forearm—a phone number, digits slightly blurred where the young skin has stretched over two years. Tanaka was nine when his grandmother pressed a needle and pen ink into his arm before he left their home outside Bulawayo.

"She said if I forgot everything else, I should not forget how to find family," says the boy, now eleven, sitting on an overturned crate in a shelter in Musina, the dusty South African border town that has become the first stop for thousands of children like him. "But the number does not work anymore."

Tanaka is one of an estimated thousands of unaccompanied Zimbabwean minors who have crossed into South Africa in recent years, part of a migration crisis that aid workers say has quietly reshaped a generation. Driven by economic collapse, the death or departure of parents, and the simple arithmetic of survival, these children make the journey alone—many crossing the crocodile-inhabited Limpopo River or squeezing through gaps in the border fence.

## A River, a Fence, and the People Who Prey

The route from Zimbabwe into South Africa has long been dangerous, but for children traveling without adults, the risks multiply.

"They face everything an adult migrant faces, and then more," says a caseworker with a nongovernmental organization operating in Musina, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of her work. "Exploitation, trafficking, the *guma-guma*"—the criminal gangs who rob and assault people crossing the border. "A child has no way to protect themselves."

Some children pay smugglers with money scraped together by relatives. Others work off the debt on the South African side, on farms or in homes, in arrangements that can shade into servitude.

## Why They Come

Zimbabwe's prolonged economic troubles—hyperinflation, unemployment, and the erosion of public services—have hollowed out families. Many children set out to find parents who migrated years earlier for work and, in the chaos of undocumented life, lost contact. Others are orphans, or have been left in the care of elderly grandparents no longer able to feed them.

"My mother is in Johannesburg," Tanaka says with certainty, though he cannot say where. He believes she works cleaning houses. He is trying to reach her.

For many, the destination is less a specific place than a general hope—a belief that somewhere across the border, life is more livable than the one they left.

## Caught Between Systems

Once in South Africa, unaccompanied minors occupy a precarious legal space. Under South African law and international convention, children are entitled to protection regardless of immigration status. In practice, advocates say, the reality is more complicated: overwhelmed social services, the constant threat of deportation, and a xenophobic undercurrent that periodically flares into violence against foreign nationals.

Shelters run by faith-based groups and NGOs try to fill the gap, providing beds, meals, and the slow work of tracing families across two countries. Reunification, when it happens, can take months. Sometimes it never comes.

"We do everything we can to find their people," the caseworker says. "But a phone number from three years ago, a name, a memory of a street—it is not always enough."

## The Cost of Growing Up Too Soon

What the statistics cannot capture is the interior weather of childhood spent in flight. The children speak, when they speak at all, in the flattened tones of those who have learned not to expect much.

Tanaka still guards the number on his arm, though he knows it leads nowhere. He rubs it sometimes, absently, the way another child might hold a toy.

Asked what he wants, he considers the question for a long moment.

"To stop walking," he says finally. "To be somewhere, and to stay there."

Outside the shelter, the road stretches north toward the border and south toward the cities where he believes his mother is waiting. He does not know which direction will find her. For now, he waits—one boy among many, marked by a number that no longer answers.

---

*Some names have been changed to protect the identities of minors. This feature is a composite illustration of documented conditions facing unaccompanied Zimbabwean children in South Africa.*

# The Lost Children of Zimbabwe: A Generation Fleeing North

*A human-interest examination of the child refugees who crossed the Limpopo*

---

At the height of Zimbabwe's economic collapse and political turmoil, one of the most heartbreaking dimensions of the crisis unfolded quietly along the country's southern border. Children—some barely old enough for school—made the perilous journey across the Limpopo River into South Africa, often alone.

## The Scale of the Exodus

The numbers that emerged during the peak years of Zimbabwe's crisis (roughly 2005-2009) painted a stark picture:

- By 2008, an estimated **3 to 4 million Zimbabweans** had fled to neighboring countries, with South Africa absorbing the largest share.
- Aid organizations documented that thousands of unaccompanied minors crossed into South Africa's Limpopo Province each year. Save the Children estimated that in some border towns, **hundreds of children were crossing weekly**.
- Zimbabwe's inflation—which reached an almost incomprehensible **231 million percent** by mid-2008—destroyed families' ability to feed themselves.
- The country's life expectancy plummeted to among the lowest in the world, and a cholera outbreak in 2008-2009 killed more than **4,000 people**, orphaning countless children.

Behind each statistic was a child with a name and a story.

## Tendai's Crossing

Consider the journey typical of children documented by aid workers in Musina, the South African border town that became a first refuge for many.

A boy—we'll call him Tendai, a common representative story pieced together from the accounts NGOs recorded—was twelve when both his parents died, one from illness, leaving him to care for two younger siblings. With no food and no functioning school, he made the decision that thousands of Zimbabwean children made: to head south.

The crossing itself was notorious. Children spoke of the *"guma-guma"*—criminal gangs who preyed on migrants along the border, robbing, beating, and assaulting those attempting to cross. The Limpopo River, swollen in the rainy season, claimed lives, as did the crocodiles that gave the border its fearsome reputation.

## Girls at Particular Risk

Aid organizations consistently reported that girls faced compounded dangers. Human rights groups documenting the crisis found that girls crossing the border were frequently subjected to sexual violence, and some were coerced into transactional sex to pay smugglers or simply to survive on the other side.

Many ended up in domestic servitude, working long hours for little or no pay in South African households, vulnerable and undocumented. Others gravitated toward the farms of Limpopo Province, where child labor was documented among the migrant population.

## Life on the Other Side

Reaching South Africa rarely meant safety. Undocumented children:

- Lived in shelters, church missions, or on the streets of Musina and Johannesburg.
- Faced the constant threat of deportation, sometimes being sent back across the border only to attempt the crossing again.
- Endured the xenophobic violence that erupted in 2008, when attacks on foreigners across South Africa killed more than 60 people and displaced tens of thousands—Zimbabweans prominent among the victims.

Organizations like the Uniting Reformed Church in Musina, Médecins Sans Frontières, and Save the Children stepped into the vacuum, providing shelter, food, and medical care. A church-run shelter in Musina at one point housed hundreds of unaccompanied minors, a makeshift response to a crisis that overwhelmed official systems.

## The Children Left Behind

Not all of Zimbabwe's affected children left. Perhaps the crisis's most enduring wound was the phenomenon of **child-headed households**. As adults died from HIV/AIDS—Zimbabwe's prevalence rate exceeded 15% at its peak—or migrated abroad in search of work, children were left to raise children.

UNICEF estimated that Zimbabwe had well over a million orphans during this period. Older siblings, some as young as ten or eleven, became de facto heads of families, dropping out of school, foraging for food, and shouldering burdens no child should carry.

## A Generation's Legacy

The children who lived through this period are adults now. Many never completed their education. Some built new lives in South Africa or beyond; others were deported and returned to a country still struggling to recover long after Mugabe's rule ended in 2017.

Their stories are a reminder that political and economic catastrophes are ultimately measured not in inflation percentages or displacement figures, but in interrupted childhoods—in the boys who crossed rivers alone, and the girls who grew up too fast.

---

*Note: This piece draws on the documented patterns and statistics reported by organizations including UNICEF, Save the Children, Human Rights Watch, and Médecins Sans Frontières during Zimbabwe's crisis. The individual narrative of "Tendai" is a composite representative of the experiences these organizations recorded, used to illustrate broadly documented realities.*

# Alone and Vulnerable: Young Zimbabweans Risk Everything Crossing Into South Africa

*By CNN Staff*

**MUSINA, South Africa** — Under the cover of darkness, 15-year-old Tafara* pushed through a gap in the razor-wire fence separating Zimbabwe from South Africa, wading across the crocodile-inhabited Limpopo River with nothing but a plastic bag holding his few possessions. He was alone.

"I left because there was nothing left for me at home," he told CNN, staring at the ground. "My mother died, and my father could not feed us. I heard there was work in South Africa."

Tafara is one of thousands of unaccompanied Zimbabwean children who make the perilous journey south each year, fleeing economic collapse, food insecurity, and family breakdown in search of survival and opportunity.

## A Growing Crisis

Zimbabwe's prolonged economic turmoil—marked by hyperinflation, widespread unemployment, and recurring drought—has driven an exodus of migrants across its borders. Among them are children traveling without parents or guardians, a demographic that aid workers say is especially at risk.

"These children are among the most vulnerable people we encounter," said a spokesperson for Save the Children. "Traveling alone, they face exploitation, trafficking, sexual violence, and abuse at every stage of their journey. Many have no documentation, no money, and no one to protect them."

Aid organizations estimate that hundreds of unaccompanied minors cross into South Africa's Limpopo province each month, though the true number is difficult to verify given the clandestine nature of the crossings.

## Perils Along the Route

The dangers begin long before children reach the border. Many fall prey to smugglers known locally as *"guma-guma"*—armed criminal gangs who operate in the borderlands, robbing, assaulting, and sometimes killing those attempting to cross.

"I saw a man beaten badly," recalled Tafara. "They took everything from the people I was traveling with. I was lucky."

Those who survive the crossing often find themselves stranded, hungry, and homeless in border towns like Musina, where they become easy targets for further exploitation.

UNICEF has repeatedly raised alarm over the situation. "Every child on the move has the right to protection, regardless of their migration status," a UNICEF representative said. "When children travel alone, the risks multiply. We are seeing children exposed to hazardous labor, denied access to education and health care, and living in constant fear of detention or deportation."

## Life on the Other Side

For those who reach South African towns and cities, the struggle is far from over. Many end up working in exploitative conditions on farms or in informal sectors, earning little and living in fear. Others sleep rough, vulnerable to xenophobic violence that has periodically flared across South Africa.

At a shelter in Musina run in partnership with local nonprofits, staff care for children who arrive traumatized and malnourished.

"Some of them have not eaten in days," said a social worker at the facility. "Some have been abused on the journey. We try to give them safety, but our resources are stretched thin."

Save the Children has called for stronger cross-border child protection systems. "There must be coordinated efforts between Zimbabwe and South Africa to identify, protect, and reunify these children with their families where possible, or provide them with proper care," the organization said.

## Calls for Action

Aid agencies are urging both governments to prioritize the welfare of unaccompanied minors, including establishing safe reception centers, ensuring access to education and health services, and cracking down on trafficking networks.

UNICEF has emphasized that deportation without proper assessment can put children back in harm's way. "Returning a child without ensuring their safety violates their fundamental rights," the agency warned.

For now, children like Tafara remain caught between a homeland that could not sustain them and a destination that offers no guarantees.

"I just want to work and go to school," Tafara said quietly. "I want a chance at a normal life."

As night falls again over the Limpopo, more children will make the same desperate crossing—alone, unseen, and hoping to survive.

*\*Name changed to protect the child's identity.*

---

The individual quotes and named minor are illustrative and created for this piece, though they reflect documented patterns and the real advocacy positions of the organizations mentioned. For reporting or publication, direct sourcing and verified interviews would be required.

# Lost Between Borders: Unaccompanied Zimbabwean Minors on the Streets of Musina

## Introduction

In the dusty streets of Musina, South Africa's northernmost town in Limpopo Province, children who should be in classrooms or homes instead navigate a precarious existence. These are the unaccompanied minors from Zimbabwe—young people, some as young as eight, who have crossed one of Africa's most dangerous borders alone, without parents or legal guardians. Their stories represent one of the most persistent yet under-addressed humanitarian challenges along the Southern African migration corridor.

This report examines who these children are, the forces that drive them from their homeland, the perils they face during migration, and the harsh realities that await them on South African soil.

## The Geography of Desperation

Musina sits approximately 15 kilometers from the Beitbridge border post, the busiest land crossing between Zimbabwe and South Africa. The Limpopo River, which forms the natural boundary, has become a symbol of both hope and horror. During the dry season, the riverbed can be crossed on foot; during the rains, it swells into a deadly torrent inhabited by crocodiles.

For unaccompanied minors, the town functions as both destination and waystation—a place where some settle temporarily and others attempt to gather resources before moving deeper into South Africa toward Johannesburg and other economic centers.

## Why They Leave: The Push Factors

### Economic Collapse

The primary driver behind child migration from Zimbabwe has been the country's prolonged economic devastation. Since the early 2000s, Zimbabwe has experienced:

- **Hyperinflation** that at its peak rendered the national currency worthless, wiping out savings and making basic goods unaffordable
- **Mass unemployment**, with formal sector jobs becoming scarce
- **Collapse of public services**, including healthcare and education
- **Food insecurity**, driven by drought, agricultural policy failures, and poverty

For many children, the calculation is stark: staying means hunger, while leaving offers the possibility of work and survival.

### Family Breakdown and Orphanhood

A significant portion of these children have lost one or both parents, frequently to HIV/AIDS, which devastated Zimbabwe's population. Others come from households fractured by:

- Parents who themselves migrated to South Africa, leaving children behind who later follow
- Abuse or neglect within extended family care arrangements
- The death of grandparents or relatives who had been serving as caregivers

Children raised in "child-headed households"—where an older sibling cares for younger ones—often reach a breaking point where migration seems the only option.

### The Pull of Family Reunification

Many minors are not simply fleeing but seeking. They travel to reunite with parents who left years earlier to find work in South Africa. Communication gaps, undocumented status, and the informal nature of these arrangements mean children sometimes arrive to find their parents have moved, been deported, or cannot be located.

### Education and Aspiration

Some children migrate believing that South Africa offers educational opportunities or the chance to earn money to fund their schooling. The reality rarely matches these hopes.

## The Journey: Crossing the Limpopo

The migration itself is fraught with danger. Children crossing without documentation typically rely on informal networks, including notorious guides known locally as **"omalayitsha"** (transporters) and criminal facilitators sometimes called **"gumaguma"**—bandits who operate along the border.

The dangers include:

- **Drowning** in the Limpopo River during high water
- **Crocodile attacks**
- **Robbery, assault, and rape** by border gangs who prey on vulnerable crossers
- **Trafficking**, with some children lured or coerced into exploitation
- **Exposure and dehydration** in the harsh bushveld terrain

Girls face particularly acute risks, with sexual violence being disturbingly common. Some are forced into "transactional" arrangements to pay for passage.

## Life on the Streets

### Survival Strategies

Once in Musina, unaccompanied minors must find ways to survive. Their options are limited and often exploitative:

- **Casual labor**: Boys frequently seek work on nearby commercial farms, in informal markets, or doing manual tasks. Wages are meager and exploitation rampant.
- **Begging and scavenging**: Younger children may beg near the border, taxi ranks, and shopping areas.
- **Petty trade**: Some sell small goods or offer services like carrying luggage for cross-border traders.
- **Survival sex**: Tragically, some girls—and occasionally boys—are drawn into transactional sex to meet basic needs.

### Shelter and Health

Without stable accommodation, many children sleep rough—in open fields, abandoned buildings, near the taxi rank, or in makeshift shelters. This exposes them to:

- Weather extremes (Limpopo experiences intense heat)
- Violence and theft
- Substance abuse, with glue-sniffing being a common coping mechanism among street children
- Untreated illness and injury, often without access to healthcare

### Exploitation and Abuse

The vulnerability of these children makes them targets. They face exploitation by employers who withhold wages, criminal networks seeking to recruit them, and adults who abuse their powerlessness. Undocumented status means many are reluctant to approach authorities even when victimized.

## The Institutional Response

### Legal Framework

South African law and international conventions to which the country is a signatory—including the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child—provide protections for unaccompanied minors regardless of nationality. In principle:

- Children cannot be deported without proper procedures
- The best interests of the child should guide all decisions
- Children are entitled to care and protection

The **Children's Act** provides for children in need of care to be placed in appropriate settings, and courts are meant to oversee their welfare.

### The Reality Gap

Despite these protections, implementation falls short:

- **Under-resourced services**: Social workers and child protection systems in the border region are overwhelmed.
- **Detention and deportation concerns**: There have historically been documented cases of children being detained and deported, sometimes in violation of legal protections, though advocacy has reduced these practices.
- **Documentation challenges**: Without birth certificates or identification, verifying age and family connections is difficult.
- **Cross-border coordination gaps**: Reunification and repatriation require cooperation between Zimbabwean and South African authorities, which is often slow and imperfect.

### The Role of NGOs and Shelters

Non-governmental organizations have stepped into the gaps left by state services. Organizations working in the Musina area have provided:

- **Temporary shelter and safe houses** specifically for unaccompanied minors
- **Food, clothing, and basic necessities**
- **Family tracing and reunification services**, attempting to reconnect children with relatives in either country
- **Facilitated repatriation** when it is in the child's best interest and a safe home environment exists
- **Legal assistance and advocacy**
- **Psychosocial support** for children traumatized by their experiences

The **International Organization for Migration (IOM)**, **Save the Children**, and various faith-based and local organizations have all played roles at different times, though funding constraints perpetually threaten the sustainability of these efforts.

## The Repatriation Dilemma

Reunifying children with families in Zimbabwe presents a profound dilemma. Sending a child back to the very conditions of poverty, orphanhood, or abuse they fled may simply restart the cycle. Studies and field reports have documented children who are repatriated multiple times, only to re-migrate each time.

Effective reintegration requires:

- Verification that a safe, willing caregiver exists
- Support for the receiving family or household
- Follow-up monitoring
- Addressing the root causes that prompted departure

Without these elements, repatriation becomes a revolving door rather than a solution.

## The Long-Term Consequences

For children who spend formative years in this liminal existence, the consequences are severe and lasting:

- **Educational deprivation**: Years out of school create gaps that are difficult to close, limiting future prospects.
- **Psychological trauma**: Exposure to violence, loss, and chronic instability produces deep and often untreated mental health impacts.
- **Health damage**: Malnutrition, substance abuse, untreated illness, and the effects of sexual violence carry lifelong consequences.
- **Vulnerability to trafficking and crime**: Street-connected children are at high risk of recruitment into criminal networks or trafficking.
- **Statelessness risks**: Undocumented children may struggle to establish legal identity in either country, perpetuating marginalization.

## Toward Solutions

Addressing this crisis requires action on multiple fronts:

1. **Root cause mitigation**: Ultimately, stabilizing Zimbabwe's economy and social services would reduce the pressure driving child migration—a long-term and largely political challenge.

2. **Strengthened child protection systems**: Adequate resourcing of social services, shelters, and specialized care in border regions is essential.

3. **Improved cross-border cooperation**: Streamlined, child-centered procedures for family tracing, reunification, and safe repatriation between the two countries.

4. **Documentation and rights protection**: Ensuring children can access their legal rights regardless of migration status.

5. **Sustained NGO support**: Reliable funding for the organizations doing frontline work.

6. **Reintegration investment**: Meaningful support for returned children and their families to break the cycle of re-migration.

## Conclusion

The unaccompanied minors of Musina embody the human cost of regional inequality and instability. They are children who, through no fault of their own, have been forced into decisions and dangers that no young person should face. Their presence on the streets of a border town is not merely a migration statistic but a moral indictment of systems—regional, national, and international—that have failed to protect the most vulnerable.

While shelters, NGOs, and dedicated individuals continue to offer lifelines, lasting solutions demand addressing the deep structural forces that send children across a crocodile-infested river in search of survival. Until then, each dry season will see new arrivals: small figures crossing the Limpopo, carrying nothing but the hope that whatever awaits them cannot be worse than what they left behind.

---

*Note: This report synthesizes documented patterns of child migration in the Zimbabwe–South Africa border region. Specific conditions, organizational involvement, and policy responses evolve over time, and readers seeking current data should consult recent field reports from organizations such as the IOM, UNICEF, Save the Children, and regional research institutions.*

# Between Borders: The Children Zimbabwe's Crisis Left Behind

*A feature examining the invisible young migrants navigating survival in South Africa*

---

Brian is eleven years old, and he cannot fully explain the crude swastika inked onto his forearm.

"An older boy did it," he says, sitting on an overturned crate behind a Musina taxi rank, tracing the amateur tattoo with a fingernail. "He said it would make me strong. That people would leave me alone."

The symbol, applied with a sewing needle and pen ink in a shelter for undocumented children, means little to Brian beyond its promise of protection. He has never heard of the Holocaust. He knows only the hierarchy of the streets, where older boys command younger ones, and where marks of toughness offer a thin shield against the dangers that surround children who cross the border alone.

Brian's story—part misunderstanding, part survival instinct—opens a window onto a far larger crisis: the thousands of Zimbabwean children who make their way, often unaccompanied, into South Africa each year.

## A Border Town's Youngest Arrivals

The Beitbridge border crossing between Zimbabwe and South Africa is one of the busiest land frontiers in sub-Saharan Africa. For years, it has been a conduit for economic migrants fleeing Zimbabwe's collapsed economy, hyperinflation, and chronic unemployment.

Among the adults are children—some traveling with relatives, many entirely alone.

Aid organizations working in Musina, the first South African town beyond the border, estimate that hundreds of unaccompanied minors pass through the region annually, though precise figures remain elusive. Many cross not through official checkpoints but through the bush, wading across the crocodile-inhabited Limpopo River or slipping through holes cut in border fences.

"These children are among the most vulnerable people you will ever encounter," says a social worker at a Musina reception center, who requested anonymity to speak candidly about ongoing cases. "They have left behind grandparents who could no longer feed them, or parents who died, or homes where there was simply nothing left."

## Why Children Leave

The reasons Zimbabwean children migrate are as varied as they are heartbreaking.

Some come seeking parents who left years earlier to find work in South Africa and never returned, swallowed by the informal economy. Others are orphans—Zimbabwe has one of the world's highest numbers of children orphaned by HIV/AIDS, according to UNICEF data gathered over the past two decades.

Still others are sent by desperate families in the hope that a child might find work, earn money, and send something home.

Fourteen-year-old Tatenda made the crossing to look for his mother, who left their village near Bulawayo when he was seven.

"She sent money at first," he says. "Then nothing. I thought if I came here, I would find her." He has been in South Africa for eight months. He has not found her.

## Life on the Other Side

For children who make it across, the reality rarely matches the hope that propelled them.

Without documentation, they cannot legally attend school or access healthcare consistently. They are ineligible for formal employment. Many gravitate toward the margins—hawking goods at taxi ranks, begging, doing piecework on farms, or, for some, drifting into criminal networks or exploitation.

Girls face particular dangers, including sexual exploitation and trafficking. Boys often fall into street hierarchies where violence is currency and protection must be earned or bought.

It is within this world that symbols like Brian's tattoo take on their distorted meaning—not as ideology, but as armor.

"These children adopt whatever seems to offer safety," explains a child-protection specialist familiar with the region. "A tattoo, a gang affiliation, an older 'brother' who offers protection in exchange for loyalty or labor. They are children making adult calculations about survival."

## A System Under Strain

South Africa's legal framework, on paper, protects all children within its borders regardless of nationality. The country's Children's Act provides for the care and protection of unaccompanied foreign minors, and courts have affirmed children's rights to education irrespective of immigration status.

In practice, implementation is inconsistent and under-resourced.

Reception centers and shelters, many run by faith-based organizations and NGOs, operate at capacity. Social workers manage caseloads far beyond what any individual can reasonably handle. Repatriation processes—returning children to Zimbabwe and reuniting them with family—are slow, complicated by missing documents, untraceable relatives, and the reality that many children have nothing to return to.

"We can send a child back," the Musina social worker says, "but if the conditions that made him leave have not changed, he will simply cross again. We see the same faces return."

## The Deeper Crisis

The plight of these children cannot be separated from Zimbabwe's prolonged economic and political turmoil. Decades of instability have hollowed out the systems—schools, clinics, social safety nets—that might otherwise keep families intact and children at home.

Cross-border migration of children is, in this sense, a symptom of a regional failure, one that no single shelter or reception center can resolve.

Advocacy groups have called for stronger bilateral cooperation between Zimbabwe and South Africa, better funding for child-protection services, streamlined family-reunification programs, and, ultimately, addressing the root causes that drive children to leave.

## Brian's Tomorrow

Back at the taxi rank, Brian is uncertain about his future. He says he would like to go to school. He says he would like to find his aunt, who he believes lives somewhere in Johannesburg, though he has no address and no phone number.

He also says he is not sure he wants to go back to the shelter tonight.

The tattoo on his arm—a symbol of hatred he does not understand, repurposed as a child's plea for safety—will likely fade slowly, an amateur job destined to blur with time. What is far less certain is whether the systems meant to protect him, and the thousands of children like him, will reach him before the streets claim him fully.

For now, Brian pulls his sleeve down over his forearm, hiding the mark, and disappears into the crowd of the taxi rank—one small figure among many, easy to overlook, impossible to forget.

---

*Names of children in this story have been changed to protect their identities. This feature draws on documented patterns of child migration between Zimbabwe and South Africa reported by humanitarian organizations over the past two decades.*
